news.titleTr: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had third alleged affair: Reuters
news.summaryTr: Reuters reported that Jensen Huang had a relationship with another Nvidia employee, hours after he resigned as CEO.
news.articleText: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had third alleged affair: Reuters Reuters reported that Jensen Huang had a relationship with another Nvidia employee, hours after he resigned as CEO. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second company employee, Reuters reported, bringing the number of alleged extramarital affairs to three. The report, citing two people familiar with the matter, followed Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO and a board member on Thursday. Reuters did not identify the other employee in its report and said attempts to reach her were unsuccessful. The two previously reported relationships involved Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence, and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Cointelegraph reached out to Nvidia for comment. US Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday during a press conference that the Justice Department had not determined whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. He confirmed that the FBI was investigating reports that she worked for the Chinese government. Beijing has denied the allegations. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% shortly after the US market opened on Thursday, trading at $151.00 as of 2:31 p.m. UTC, according to Yahoo Finance. Venture capitalist Haseeb Qureshi argued that the mounting disclosures undermined Huang’s credibility, pushing back against tech industry figures defending the Nvidia co-founder. “As others have said: ‘when you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate for the ants in your kitchen is not two,’” Qureshi wrote on X. Related: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, exits board; shares plunge

news.title: Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low
news.summary: Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low
news.summaryTr: Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump.
news.articleText: Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump. Crypto exchange Gemini has just reported its lowest quarterly retail trading volume in three years, despite an increase in overall crypto trading volume. Total spot trading volume rose 18% from the second quarter to $4.5 billion, according to Gemini’s Q3 earnings report. Institutional volume climbed 26% to $3.9 billion, while retail volume fell 14% to $600 million, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023. Gemini said the quarterly increase in spot trading volume was “supported by increased institutional Zcash activity and expanded affiliated market-making,” but did not give a specific reason for the decline in retail trading. Despite the retail slump, Gemini’s exchange revenue increased 7% from the previous quarter to $13.4 million as institutional revenue more than doubled. Retail traders remained its largest source of exchange revenue, contributing nearly three-quarters of the total. Crypto exchanges turn to prediction markets for growth A number of crypto exchanges also reported softer crypto trading activity in the most recent quarter. Coinbase reported softer retail and institutional activity, with consumer spot trading volume falling 9% from the previous quarter to $23.4 billion. Coinbase chief financial officer Alesia Haas said “continued growth in prediction markets helped offset softer crypto trading activity.” At Robinhood, crypto revenue fell 55% year-on-year to $120 million, offset by a sixfold increase in event-contract revenue to $173 million. Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off Gemini also got some help from its own prediction exchange, Gemini Predictions, with revenue from that business unit increasing 52% quarter-on-quarter to $796,000, though it wasn’t significant enough to offset declines elsewhere. Gemini looks to expand prediction markets Gemini reported stronger prediction-market activity heading into the fourth quarter, with average daily traders in October running about 50% above the third-quarter average. Nearly a third of new prediction traders were new to Gemini, more than double the proportion in Q3. The company is also seeking to distribute its event contracts through other platforms. An August nonbinding agreement with Apex Fintech Solutions would make Gemini Titan the exclusive venue for crypto event contracts distributed through Apex’s futures brokerage to its brokerage customers, subject to definitive agreements. Gemini is set to host a Q3 earnings call on Friday. Magazine: NK hackers join memecoin trenches, xStocks adds Hong Kong equities: Asia Express

news.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
news.summary: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
news.summaryTr: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
news.articleText: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over? - Published Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022. But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force. Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements. Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority. Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat. "The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage." Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says. Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost. Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC. He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy." The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability. It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored. Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes. Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days. "We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active. Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents. The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds. Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded. Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC. Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations. However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael. Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF." He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says. Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says. What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded." While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours." In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF. However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict. "First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF." Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade. Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement. In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters. "If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says. Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says. Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government. However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence. In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace. "Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle. news.articleTextTr: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over? - Published Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022. But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force. Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements. Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority. Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat. "The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage." Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says. Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost. Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC. He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy." The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability. It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored. Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes. Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days. "We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active. Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents. The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds. Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded. Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC. Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations. However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael. Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF." He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says. Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says. What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded." While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours." In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF. However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict. "First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF." Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade. Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement. In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters. "If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says. Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says. Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government. However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence. In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace. "Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle. news.titleTr: Cevdet Yılmaz'dan COP31 mesajı: "Özel sektör olmadan iklim hedeflerine ulaşılamaz"
news.summaryTr: Antalya’da düzenlenen COP31 İş ve Yatırım Zirvesi’nde 55’i aşkın ülkeden bin 500’ün üzerinde katılımcı bir araya geldi. Zirvede iklim finansmanı, enerji güvenliği ve sanayinin yeşil dönüşümü öne çıkarken, iş dünyasının iklim hedeflerinin hayata geçirilmesindeki rolüne dikkat çekildi.
news.articleText: Cevdet Yılmaz'dan COP31 mesajı: "Özel sektör olmadan iklim hedeflerine ulaşılamaz" - Antalya'da düzenlenen COP31 İş ve Yatırım Zirvesi'nde 55'i aşkın ülkeden bin 500’ün üzerinde katılımcı bir araya geldi. - Zirvede iklim finansmanı, enerji güvenliği ve sanayinin yeşil dönüşümü öne çıkarken, iş dünyasının iklim hedeflerinin hayata geçirilmesindeki rolüne dikkat çekildi. Türkiye Odalar ve Borsalar Birliği (TOBB) koordinasyonunda düzenlenen COP31 İş ve Yatırım Zirvesi, 12 Kasım’da Antalya’da başladı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle "Hedeften Uygulamaya" temasıyla gerçekleştirilen zirvede, iklim hedeflerinin yatırım projelerine dönüştürülmesi, enerji dönüşümü, sanayinin karbonsuzlaştırılması ve dirençli şehirler ele alındı. Zirvenin açılışında konuşan Cumhurbaşkanı Yardımcısı Cevdet Yılmaz, yeşil dönüşümün fosil yakıt ithalatını azaltarak makroekonomik istikrara katkı sağlayacağını belirtti. İklim hedeflerine ulaşılması için finansmana hazır projelerin ve kamu-özel sektör iş birliğinin önemini vurgulayan Yılmaz, özel sektörün sürece dahil edilmediği iklim politikalarının başarılı olamayacağını söyledi. COP31 Başkanı ve Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanı Murat Kurum ise zirveyi bir “uygulama COP’u” olarak konumlandırdıklarını ifade etti. Kurum, 2035’e kadar nihai enerji tüketiminde elektriğin payını yüzde 35’e, üretim ve imalatta döngüsel malzeme kullanımını en az yüzde 15’e çıkarma hedeflerini açıkladı. İklim Uygulama Köprüsü aracılığıyla ülkelerin önceliklerini yatırım yapılabilir projelere dönüştürmeyi amaçladıklarını belirtti. Hisarcıklıoğlu: "İklim eylemi en büyük yatırım fırsatı" TOBB Başkanı ve COP31 İş Forumu Başkanı Rifat Hisarcıklıoğlu, iklim hedeflerine müzakere salonlarında değil, fabrikalarda, tarlalarda ve şantiyelerde ulaşılabileceğini söyledi. İş dünyasının iklim eylemi açısından merkezi bir rol üstlendiğini belirten Hisarcıklıoğlu, iklim eyleminin bir maliyet değil, neslin en büyük yatırım fırsatı olduğunu vurguladı. Hisarcıklıoğlu, bu fırsatın hayata geçirilmesi için teknolojinin yanı sıra net ve istikrarlı politikalara, hızlı izin süreçlerine ve adil rekabete ihtiyaç duyulduğunu kaydetti. Dünya Bankası Başkanı'ndan özel sektör sermayesi vurgusu Zirvede düzenlenen oturumda konuşan Dünya Bankası Grubu Başkanı Ajay Banga, iklim yatırımlarının ekonomik getiriler ve genç istihdamı odağında değerlendirilmesi gerektiğini belirtti. BBVA Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı Carlos Torres Vila ise gelişmekte olan ülkelerde KOBİ’lerin yeşil finansmana erişiminin önemine dikkat çekti. Vila, enerji verimliliği, elektrifikasyon, akıllı şebekeler ve yapay zekanın Türkiye gibi yüksek potansiyele sahip ülkelerin rekabet gücünü artırabileceğini ifade etti. Enerji güvenliği ve sanayinin dönüşümü gündemde Zirvenin oturumlarında enerji arz güvenliği, elektrifikasyon, iklim yatırımlarının finansmanı ve sanayinin karbonsuzlaştırılması da ele alındı. Enerji ve Tabii Kaynaklar Bakanı Alparslan Bayraktar, IEA İcra Direktörü Fatih Birol ve BBVA Grup CEO’su Onur Genç enerji güvenliğini değerlendirirken, Sanayi ve Teknoloji Bakanı Mehmet Fatih Kacır ile Sabancı Holding CEO’su Kıvanç Zaimler elektrifikasyon başlığında görüşlerini paylaştı. Londra Belediye Başkanı Sadiq Khan ise şehirlerin iklim mücadelesindeki rolüne dikkat çekerek, dünya nüfusunun yarısından fazlasının şehirlerde yaşadığını ve enerjinin yüzde 70’inden fazlasının şehirlerde tüketildiğini söyledi. Khan, şehirlerin iklim krizinde ya sorunun parçası ya da çözümün kendisi olabileceğini ifade etti. COP31 İş ve Yatırım Zirvesi, 13 Kasım’da döngüsel ekonomi, KOBİ’lerin yeşil dönüşümü, iklim teknolojileri ve COP32 sürecine ilişkin oturumlarla devam edecek.

news.titleTr: Trump'tan Küba'ya gözdağı: "Görev sürem bitmeden halletmek istiyorum"
news.summaryTr: ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, Küba'ya yönelik askeri müdahale seçeneğini dışlamadı. Trump, 2028'de görev süresi sona ermeden önce Küba meselesini çözmek istediğini söyledi.
news.articleText: Trump'tan Küba'ya gözdağı: "Görev sürem bitmeden halletmek istiyorum" - ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, Küba'ya yönelik askeri müdahale seçeneğini dışlamadı. Trump, 2028'de görev süresi sona ermeden önce Küba meselesini çözmek istediğini söyledi. ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, Küba'ya yönelik olası bir askeri operasyon hakkında açıklamalarda bulundu. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Salem News Channel'a telefonla bağlanan Trump, görev süresi dolmadan önce Küba meselesini halletmek istediğini belirtti. Küba'yı "başarısız bir ülke" olarak nitelendiren Trump, ABD Dışişleri Bakanı Marco Rubio'nun süreci iyi yönettiğini ve gelişmeleri yakından takip ettiklerini söyledi. Küba'ya askeri güç kullanılıp kullanılmayacağına ilişkin soruyu yanıtlayan Trump, sınırlı bir operasyon seçeneğine de açık olduğunu ifade etti. Trump, "Bunun için biraz askeri güç gerekse, zayıf bir operasyon olsa bile, sizin için sorun olur mu?" sorusuna, "Benim için uygundur, bunu kesinlikle değerlendiririm." yanıtını verdi. ABD ile Küba arasındaki ilişkiler, 1959 Küba Devrimi'nden bu yana ambargo ve siyasi gerilimlerle şekilleniyor. Washington yönetimi, 1960'lardan itibaren Küba'ya yönelik ekonomik yaptırımlar uyguluyor.

news.titleTr: Zayıflama ilaçlarında kalıcı görme kaybı riski: FDA'dan yeni uyarı
news.summaryTr: FDA, Ozempic, Wegovy ve Mounjaro gibi popüler diyabet ve zayıflama ilaçlarının nadir ancak kalıcı görme kaybına yol açabilen bir göz rahatsızlığıyla ilişkili olabileceği uyarısıyla güvenlik etiketlerine yeni bilgiler eklenmesini istedi.
news.articleText: Zayıflama ilaçlarında kalıcı görme kaybı riski: FDA'dan yeni uyarı - FDA, Ozempic, Wegovy ve Mounjaro gibi popüler diyabet ve zayıflama ilaçlarının nadir ancak kalıcı görme kaybına yol açabilen bir göz rahatsızlığıyla ilişkili olabileceği uyarısıyla güvenlik etiketlerine yeni bilgiler eklenmesini istedi. ABD Gıda ve İlaç Dairesi (FDA), diyabet tedavisinde ve kilo verme amacıyla kullanılan bazı popüler ilaçların nadir görülen ve kalıcı görme kaybına neden olabilen bir göz hastalığıyla ilişkili olabileceği uyarısında bulundu. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Kurum, GLP-1 grubu ilaçların güvenlik etiketlerine olası riske ilişkin yeni uyarılar eklenmesini zorunlu kıldı. FDA'nın açıklamasına göre, glukagon benzeri peptit-1 reseptör agonisti (GLP-1 RA) grubundaki ilaçlar, "arteritik olmayan anterior iskemik optik nöropati" (NAION) adı verilen göz rahatsızlığıyla bağlantılı olabilir. Görme sinirine giden kan akışının azalmasıyla ortaya çıkan NAION, genellikle tek gözde ani ve ağrısız görme kaybına yol açıyor. Açıklamada, mevcut tedavilerle kaybedilen görmeyi geri kazandırdığı bilinen bir yöntemin bulunmadığı belirtildi. Birçok ilacın etiketine eklenecek FDA, Novo Nordisk'in Ozempic ve Wegovy, Eli Lilly'nin Mounjaro ve Zepbound ile Sanofi'nin Soliqua ilaçları dahil olmak üzere GLP-1 etkisi gösteren tüm ilaçların güvenlik etiketlerinde olası riske yer verilmesini istedi. news.summary: Elon Musk'ın uzay şirketi SpaceX, Texas ve Arizona'da kurulması planlanan iki süper bilgisayar tesisi için 74 milyar dolardan fazla yatırım yapmayı hedefliyor. Projelerin binlerce kişiye istihdam sağlaması bekleniyor.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: SpaceX'ten iki eyalette dev yatırım: 74 milyar doları aşacak
news.summaryTr: Elon Musk'ın uzay şirketi SpaceX, Texas ve Arizona'da kurulması planlanan iki süper bilgisayar tesisi için 74 milyar dolardan fazla yatırım yapmayı hedefliyor. Projelerin binlerce kişiye istihdam sağlaması bekleniyor.
news.articleText: SpaceX'ten iki eyalette dev yatırım: 74 milyar doları aşacak - Elon Musk'ın uzay şirketi SpaceX, Texas ve Arizona'da kurulması planlanan iki süper bilgisayar tesisi için 74 milyar dolardan fazla yatırım yapmayı hedefliyor. - Projelerin binlerce kişiye istihdam sağlaması bekleniyor. SpaceX, ABD'nin Texas ve Arizona eyaletlerinde iki büyük süper bilgisayar tesisi kurmak için toplam 74 milyar doları aşan yatırım planını duyurdu. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Şirketin açıklamasına göre, Texas'ın Rio Grande Vadisi'ndeki Starbase bölgesine 24 milyar doların üzerinde, Arizona'nın Cochise County bölgesine ise yaklaşık 50 milyar dolarlık yatırım yapılacak. Texas projesi 3 binden fazla kişiye iş sağlayacak SpaceX, Starbase'de süper bilgisayar altyapısı için planlanan yatırımın inşaat aşamasında 3 binden fazla kişiye istihdam sağladığını, tesis faaliyete geçtiğinde ise 500'den fazla kalıcı iş oluşturmasının beklendiğini bildirdi. Tesisin kendi elektriğini üreteceği belirtilirken, Brownsville kentinin su ve atık su altyapısının genişletilmesi için 220 milyon dolarlık yatırım taahhüt edildi. Arizona'da 50 milyar dolarlık tesis Arizona'daki projenin inşaat aşamasında yaklaşık 5 bin 500, işletme döneminde ise 1000 kalıcı istihdam yaratması öngörülüyor. SpaceX, yerel elektrik kooperatifleriyle yürütülecek projeyle enerji altyapısının güçlendirilmesini ve elektrik faturalarının potansiyel olarak yüzde 20'ye kadar düşürülmesini hedefliyor. Tesisin kuru soğutma sistemiyle çalışacağı ve endüstriyel amaçlarla yer altı suyu kullanılmayacağı belirtildi. Starbase kentinde ayrıca doğalgazla çalışan bir elektrik santrali kurulması planlanıyor. Projeye ilişkin emlak vergisi indirimi ve ekonomik kalkınma anlaşmasının 9 Aralık'ta yapılacak Kent Komisyonu toplantısında değerlendirilmesi bekleniyor.

news.titleTr: Borsa İstanbul'da 5 şirket yeni iş ilişkisi duyurdu: İşte KAP'a bildirilen sözleşme detayları
news.summaryTr: Borsa İstanbul’da 12 Kasım'da 5 şirket yeni iş ilişkisi, sözleşme, yatırım, varlık satışı ve ihale gelişmelerini duyurdu. Açıklamalarda milyonlarca dolarlık ve milyarlarca liralık işlemler öne çıktı.
news.articleText: Borsa İstanbul'da 5 şirket yeni iş ilişkisi duyurdu: İşte KAP'a bildirilen sözleşme detayları Borsa İstanbul’da 12 Kasım'da 5 şirket yeni iş ilişkisi, sözleşme, yatırım, varlık satışı ve ihale gelişmelerini duyurdu. Açıklamalarda milyonlarca dolarlık ve milyarlarca liralık işlemler öne çıktı. GESAN'dan 171,6 milyon TL'lik ilave sipariş Girişim Elektrik, daha önce imzaladığı reaktif güç kompanzasyon sistemleri sözleşmeleri kapsamında Başkent EDAŞ ve Toroslar EDAŞ'tan ilave sipariş aldı. Vergiler hariç siparişlerin 26,76 milyon TL'lik kısmı işçilik, 2,88 milyon dolarlık (güncel kurla 171,58 milyon TL) kısmı ise malzeme tedarikinden oluştu. Malzeme kapsamındaki ürünlerin, şirketin bağlı ortaklığı Europower Enerji tarafından üretileceği bildirildi. TCKRC 173 milyon TL'lik ihaleyi kazandı Kıraç Galvaniz, 23 Ekim 2026'da gerçekleştirilen Karayolları 4. Bölge Müdürlüğünün çelik otokorkuluk yapım ihalesinin şirket uhdesinde kaldığını açıkladı. 173 milyon TL bedelli ihaleye ilişkin kesinleşme kararı şirkete ulaştı. Nihai sözleşme sürecine ilişkin gelişmelerin kamuoyuyla paylaşılacağı bildirildi. MİA Teknoloji'den TCDD projesinde 18,3 milyon TL'lik tamamlanma MİA Teknoloji, TCDD 4. Bölge Müdürlüğü sorumluluk alanındaki demiryolu hatlarının mobil haritalama yöntemiyle envanter tespiti ve ölçümüne ilişkin projeyi tamamladı. İş artışı ve KDV dahil projenin toplam tamamlanma bedeli 18 milyon 349 bin 470,24 TL oldu. Şirket, projenin kabul işlemlerinin de sonuçlandığını bildirdi. KARÇEL'den 19,8 milyon euroluk yatırım kredisi Kardemir Çelik, Haddehane Modernizasyon Projesi kapsamında DZ Bank AG ile 19 milyon 774 bin 166 euro tutarında kredi sözleşmesi imzaladı. Çin İhracat ve Kredi Sigorta Kuruluşu Sinosure sigortası kapsamında sağlanan kredinin geri ödeme vadesi 12 yıl olarak belirlendi. Şirket, yatırımla üretim altyapısını modernize etmeyi, operasyonel verimliliği artırmayı ve üretimin çevresel etkilerini azaltmayı hedefliyor. Yatırımın orta ve uzun vadede maliyet yapısı ile kârlılığa katkı sağlaması bekleniyor. ORGE'nin hastane projesinde sözleşme büyüklüğü arttı Orge Enerji, devam eden Anatolia Antalya ve Anatolia Alanya Hastaneleri Projesi'nde sözleşme büyüklüğünün arttığını açıkladı. Buna göre, başlangıçta 589 bin 712 euro ve 46 milyon 77 bin 269 TL olan sözleşme tutarı, kesilen faturalarla 1 milyon 180 bin 885 euro ve 92 milyon 973 bin 275 TL'ye ulaştı.

items.title: Australian footballers will not be charged after hotel incident, police say
items.summary: Four Sydney Swans players had been under investigation after an alleged sexual assault after a game in Melbourne.

items.titleTr: Australian footballers will not be charged after hotel incident, police say
items.summaryTr: Four Sydney Swans players had been under investigation after an alleged sexual assault after a game in Melbourne.
items.articleText: Sydney Swans players will not be charged after hotel incident, police say - Published Four top Australian Football League (AFL) players who were investigated in relation to an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne earlier this year will not be charged, police have said. After a "thorough investigation and based on legal advice" police would not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence", police said in a statement. Four Sydney Swans players - Isaac Heeney, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who now plays for North Melbourne - had been suspended for the rest of the season over the incident in August. The men previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards by inviting women back to the hotel after a game and drinking. Australian media reported that three women, understood to be adult entertainers, had alleged inappropriate touching during the incident at the Pullman Hotel and are looking into civil action. "Due to the ongoing civil matter, Victoria Police is unable to make further comment," police said in a statement on Friday. A fifth player, Riley Bice, who was also suspended by the club, had already been cleared by police. A lawyer for one of the women said she was "devastated" by the police decision. Jackson Pannam, of Slater and Gordon law firm, added that the move "does not amount to a finding that the incident our client reported did not occur, nor does it diminish the seriousness of what she says happened or its profound impact on her". John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, acting for the other two women, told the ABC his clients were "very disappointed and distressed". They would "vigorously pursue" a civil action, he said. "My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said. Heeney welcomed the police announcement, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult for my family, [my fiancee] Steffie and those close to me". "To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice," he continued. The Swans said in a statement that it had been "clear from the outset" that its decision to suspend the players was "separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision". "The Club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," it said. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich told reporters it was "not a day for anyone to really celebrate" and "we're still looking very hard at the programme and understanding where we need to get better". He said the club would be doing everything to "restore the standards that this club has held for a long period of time". In a separate statement the AFL acknowledged the police decision and said it reserved the right to investigate should any further relevant information come to light.

items.title: Scandal-hit Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits, plunging AI chipmaking giant into turmoil
items.summary: US lawmakers now want to question him over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Scandal-hit Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits, plunging AI chipmaking giant into turmoil
items.summaryTr: US lawmakers now want to question him over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
items.articleText: Scandal-hit Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits, plunging AI chipmaking giant into turmoil - Published Jensen Huang has abruptly quit as chief executive of AI chipmaking giant Nvidia after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill. Nvidia is now under scrutiny from US lawmakers in Washington DC demanding Huang answer questions over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy. One of the world's most valuable companies as a result of the AI boom, Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines. Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, called an emergency meeting of her executive team to discuss the company's future. His alleged conduct not only potentially crossed professional boundaries, but has made Nvidia the target of questions from US politicians who have expressed concern about national security risks. Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang. On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive. Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear. And US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons, along with other Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, publicly demanded that Huang brief Congress on the matter. If he refuses to appear voluntarily before any committee that calls him, he could be subpoenaed, one Senate staff member told the BBC. Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday. According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company. Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close. Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company. It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said. Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public. Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared. Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information. The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures. Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming. But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data. Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO. Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires. He is far from the first tech titan to become embroiled in revelations of infidelity. Bill Gates of Microsoft and Jeff Bezos of Amazon had affairs exposed in the last decade. Both men are now divorced from their wives. Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia. Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago. Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector. Because of Nvidia's size and success in recent years, such a drop can have a direct impact on the savings accounts of ordinary Americans. Nvidia's value makes up about 7% of the S&P 500 index. That index is offered as a popular index fund in US retirement savings accounts. Those account balances rise and fall with the changes of the stock market. Related topics - Published11 hours ago

items.title: Microsoft struggling to restore service as global outage affects Outlook and Teams
items.summary: Microsoft said the outage was caused by servers unexpected becoming unavailable, straining other systems.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Microsoft struggling to restore service as global outage affects Outlook and Teams
items.summaryTr: Microsoft said the outage was caused by servers unexpected becoming unavailable, straining other systems.
items.articleText: Microsoft struggling to restore service as global outage affects Outlook and Teams - Published Microsoft is struggling to fix a major global outage of its service that is reportedly affecting tens of thousands of users. Services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot have been affected by "connectivity problems". The company said in a series of updates on X that it was seeing "positive results" with its efforts to restore services and that it was rushing to fix the problem. Reports of issues with Outlook peaked globally at nearly 140,000 around 18:00 GMT on Thursday, according to monitoring website Downdetector. The BBC understands there is no indication the outage was caused by a cyber-attack. The disruption affects programs that are part of Microsoft 365 - a popular online service among businesses that allows them to use workplace tools like Outlook, Teams and OneDrive. For international organisations, this platform is essential for connecting and collaborating with colleagues around the world. Among the issues, users may be unable to view certain files or details on their calendar apps, Microsoft said. Its AI platform, Copilot, may also be unable to work properly. Messaging and online meetings were largely functional, the firm added. Microsoft said on X that the outage was caused by a number of servers "being unexpectedly unavailable", straining its remaining systems. "We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible," said a Microsoft spokesperson. The company later warned that some services that had been restored "can become unresponsive again", adding that customers "in any region" could be affected. Users around the world including the US, Japan and Singapore have reported facing disruptions. AI companies feel the impact The outage has hit other companies, including AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, which work with Microsoft's systems. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected. Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected the tech giant's suite of productivity tools and companies worldwide. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled it to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

items.titleTr: Trump nominates Hester Peirce successor among SEC, CFTC picks
items.summaryTr: The White House also named a former CFTC commissioner and two CLARITY Act veterans as nominees to fill vacancies at the SEC and CFTC.
items.articleText: Trump nominates Hester Peirce successor among SEC, CFTC picks The White House also named a former CFTC commissioner and two CLARITY Act veterans as nominees to fill vacancies at the SEC and CFTC. US President Donald Trump has nominated Steven Levine to replace former Securities and Exchange Commission Commissioner Hester Peirce, one of the agency’s most prominent crypto advocates, as part of four nominations to fill vacancies at the SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The White House’s latest announcement on Thursday named two nominees each for the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, agencies whose decisions help shape US cryptocurrency regulation, among other functions. All four nominations require Senate confirmation. The nominations would replenish several commissioner roles. The SEC currently has only two of its five commissioner seats filled, while CFTC Chairman Michael Selig is the sole member of his agency’s five-seat commission. The nominations come weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the Senate in January, giving a narrow window for Republicans to confirm Trump’s picks. Related: House Finance panel chair says regulator actions on crypto ‘fall short’ of CLARITY bill Levine, a Republican, was nominated for an SEC term ending June 5, 2030, replacing Peirce, who left the agency in October. Peirce was a leading advocate for clearer crypto rules at the SEC, helping shape its approach to digital assets as the former head of its Crypto Task Force, while Levine’s views on crypto regulation are less publicly established. Trump also nominated Democrat Kristin Johnson, a former CFTC commissioner, for the SEC seat held by Caroline Crenshaw, whose term has also expired. Johnson’s proposed term ends June 5, 2029. Johnson has advocated for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules for crypto firms in her time at the CFTC. For the CFTC, Trump nominated Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland, both of whom worked on the Clarity Act. CFTC Chairman Mike Selig called them “two strong bipartisan picks” for CFTC commissioners and said he looked forward to working with them upon their confirmation. The nominees would typically appear before the Senate Banking Committee for the SEC positions and the Senate Agriculture Committee for the CFTC roles. items.summary: The Ukrainian president says it makes sense for European leaders to be involved as Ukraine hopes to eventually join the EU.

items.titleTr: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
items.summaryTr: The Ukrainian president says it makes sense for European leaders to be involved as Ukraine hopes to eventually join the EU.
items.articleText: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks - Published Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia. European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations. Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed. The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war. But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given. - US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow - Published6 hours ago - Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine - Published12 hours ago Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union. On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important." He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table". "He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added. Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent. Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player". Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal. Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war. "Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common. Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky. Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones. The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

items.summaryTr: Reuters reported that Jensen Huang had a relationship with another Nvidia employee, hours after he resigned as CEO.
items.articleText: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had third alleged affair: Reuters Reuters reported that Jensen Huang had a relationship with another Nvidia employee, hours after he resigned as CEO. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second company employee, Reuters reported, bringing the number of alleged extramarital affairs to three. The report, citing two people familiar with the matter, followed Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO and a board member on Thursday. Reuters did not identify the other employee in its report and said attempts to reach her were unsuccessful. The two previously reported relationships involved Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence, and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Cointelegraph reached out to Nvidia for comment. US Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday during a press conference that the Justice Department had not determined whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. He confirmed that the FBI was investigating reports that she worked for the Chinese government. Beijing has denied the allegations. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% shortly after the US market opened on Thursday, trading at $151.00 as of 2:31 p.m. UTC, according to Yahoo Finance. Venture capitalist Haseeb Qureshi argued that the mounting disclosures undermined Huang’s credibility, pushing back against tech industry figures defending the Nvidia co-founder. “As others have said: ‘when you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate for the ants in your kitchen is not two,’” Qureshi wrote on X. Related: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, exits board; shares plunge

items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low
items.summaryTr: Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump.
items.articleText: Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump. Crypto exchange Gemini has just reported its lowest quarterly retail trading volume in three years, despite an increase in overall crypto trading volume. Total spot trading volume rose 18% from the second quarter to $4.5 billion, according to Gemini’s Q3 earnings report. Institutional volume climbed 26% to $3.9 billion, while retail volume fell 14% to $600 million, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023. Gemini said the quarterly increase in spot trading volume was “supported by increased institutional Zcash activity and expanded affiliated market-making,” but did not give a specific reason for the decline in retail trading. Despite the retail slump, Gemini’s exchange revenue increased 7% from the previous quarter to $13.4 million as institutional revenue more than doubled. Retail traders remained its largest source of exchange revenue, contributing nearly three-quarters of the total. Crypto exchanges turn to prediction markets for growth A number of crypto exchanges also reported softer crypto trading activity in the most recent quarter. Coinbase reported softer retail and institutional activity, with consumer spot trading volume falling 9% from the previous quarter to $23.4 billion. Coinbase chief financial officer Alesia Haas said “continued growth in prediction markets helped offset softer crypto trading activity.” At Robinhood, crypto revenue fell 55% year-on-year to $120 million, offset by a sixfold increase in event-contract revenue to $173 million. Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off Gemini also got some help from its own prediction exchange, Gemini Predictions, with revenue from that business unit increasing 52% quarter-on-quarter to $796,000, though it wasn’t significant enough to offset declines elsewhere. Gemini looks to expand prediction markets Gemini reported stronger prediction-market activity heading into the fourth quarter, with average daily traders in October running about 50% above the third-quarter average. Nearly a third of new prediction traders were new to Gemini, more than double the proportion in Q3. The company is also seeking to distribute its event contracts through other platforms. An August nonbinding agreement with Apex Fintech Solutions would make Gemini Titan the exclusive venue for crypto event contracts distributed through Apex’s futures brokerage to its brokerage customers, subject to definitive agreements. Gemini is set to host a Q3 earnings call on Friday. Magazine: NK hackers join memecoin trenches, xStocks adds Hong Kong equities: Asia Express

items.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
items.summary: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
items.summaryTr: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
items.articleText: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over? - Published Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022. But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force. Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements. Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority. Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat. "The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage." Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says. Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost. Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC. He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy." The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability. It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored. Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes. Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days. "We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active. Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents. The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds. Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded. Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC. Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations. However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael. Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF." He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says. Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says. What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded." While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours." In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF. However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict. "First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF." Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade. Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement. In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters. "If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says. Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says. Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government. However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence. In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace. "Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle. items.articleTextTr: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over? - Published Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022. But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force. Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements. Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority. Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat. "The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage." Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says. Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost. Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC. He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy." The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability. It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored. Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes. "We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active. Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents. The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
